pedagogy.summary: Children solve word problems about collections of US coins and bills — finding the total value, making change, and writing amounts with the $ and ¢ symbols appropriately. The deep difficulty is that a coin's value is ABSTRACT and matches neither its physical size nor the number of coins: a dime is smaller than a nickel yet worth more, and three dimes beat five pennies. Money is best taught as a MEASURE of value (like length or weight), using proportional manipulatives that make each coin's worth visible, introducing coins two denominations at a time to limit switches of counting pattern, and first building the skip-counting and place-value number sense that totalling coins depends on.
bestPractices: Treat money as measuring value — begin with barter and non-standard units so children feel why standard values are needed (Fanelli & Tracy)
Use PROPORTIONAL manipulatives (a dime shown as ten unit-squares) rather than realistic play coins, because a coin is not a concrete representation of its own value
Introduce coins two denominations at a time to reduce cognitive load and limit how often the counting pattern must switch
Build the underlying number sense first — skip-counting by 5s, 10s, 25s and place value — since totalling mixed coins is a skip-count-and-switch task
Teach 'counting on' from the largest coin; model correct $ and ¢ notation and when each is used (100¢ = $1)
keyRepresentations: Proportional value strips / 'proportional dollar' (a coin laid over its worth in unit-squares)
A number line or hundred-square for skip-counting coin values
A coin-value reference (penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, dollar 100¢)
A part-whole bar for making change (cost and amount paid)
commonMisconceptions: Value = size: a bigger coin is worth more (nickel > dime; five pennies > three dimes)
Value = count: each coin counts as one, or all coins are counted by ones regardless of denomination (unitary thinking)
Cannot switch counting patterns — counts 25, 50, 75 then cannot shift to +10 for a dime or +1 for a penny
Notation errors — mixing $ and ¢ ($0.50¢, or $5 for a nickel), or writing 5¢ as $5
Overusing one denomination (all dimes) because counting by tens is easiest, rather than realistic combinations

learn.summary: Children solve word problems with US coins and bills — totalling value, making change, and writing amounts with $ and ¢ correctly. The core difficulty is that a coin's value is abstract and matches neither its physical size nor the number of coins (a dime is smaller than a nickel yet worth more; three dimes beat five pennies). Money is best taught as a measure of value using proportional representations that make each coin's worth visible, introducing denominations a couple at a time, and first building the skip-counting and place-value number sense that totalling mixed coins depends on.

activities.title: Proportional-coin workbench: build value and make change
feedback: When a learner picks the bigger or more-numerous set as worth more, lay each coin over its unit-squares so the 10 squares of the dime stand beside the 5 of the nickel — let the squares, not the coin size, settle it.
If a learner counts every coin by ones (2 dimes + 3 pennies = '5'), highlight that one dime is already 10 squares; start from a single denomination before mixing.
When a learner stalls switching from 25s to 10s to 1s (counts 25, 50, 75 then says '76' for a dime), model counting on from the largest coin and track the running total on a number line.
For a correct total reached by counting on, ask them to remake the same amount with different coins to confirm value, not a fixed coin set, is what matters.
activities.rationale: Fanelli & Tracy report that children equate value with size and that coins are not concrete representations of their own value, recommending proportional manipulatives over realistic play coins and teaching money as a measure of value. A running total that accumulates by value supports 'counting on' and switching counting patterns, which Chandler & Kamii link to the difficulty of coordinating tens and ones when making change (that source is marked unverified in the row). The side-by-side square comparison is a proposed way to target the size/number heuristics through what the learner sees and does.
sourceClaims: Children often equate value with size — believing nickels are worth more than dimes and that five pennies are more valuable than three dimes — because relative coin sizes do not correlate with relative values; coins are therefore NOT concrete representations of their value, so proportional manipulatives are recommended over realistic play coins, money should be taught as a measure of value, and these size-based misconceptions lessen around ages 7-8, making second grade the appropriate time for formal money instruction.

Giving change when payment is made with a dime is difficult for young children because of the difficulty of coordinating tens and ones — underlying the trouble children have switching counting patterns across denominations.

Grade 2 standard: solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately (e.g. if you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?).
learnerActions: Place coins onto a mat; as each coin is placed, it opens into its worth shown as unit-squares (dime = 10 squares, nickel = 5, penny = 1, quarter = 25) while a running total counts on by value.
Set the small dime beside the fatter nickel and compare the stacks of squares: the dime's 10 squares visibly outstretch the nickel's 5.
Build a target amount such as 30¢ in more than one way (e.g. three dimes; or a quarter and a nickel) and compare the coins used.
Switch to a make-change task: an item costs 40¢; pay with coins totalling 46¢ and count up the 6¢ change.
Count a mixed handful (2 dimes and 3 pennies) by counting on from the largest coin: 10, 20, then 21, 22, 23.
activities.intendedInsight: A coin's worth is a number of cents you count on, separate from the coin's size or how many coins there are; proportional value makes 'smaller but worth more' visible and concrete.

activities.title: Coin denomination reference with the size/worth contradiction
feedback: If a learner guesses worth from size, draw attention to the stated value and the dime-vs-nickel fact.
Reinforce 100¢ = $1 so a nickel is written 5¢, never $5.
activities.rationale: Securing denomination values and surfacing the size/worth contradiction gives a foundation for totalling. This is exposition that establishes facts; on its own it does not provide totalling or make-change practice, so it is best used before or alongside the workbench rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Children often equate value with size — believing nickels are worth more than dimes and that five pennies are more valuable than three dimes — because relative coin sizes do not correlate with relative values; coins are therefore NOT concrete representations of their value, so proportional manipulatives are recommended over realistic play coins, money should be taught as a measure of value, and these size-based misconceptions lessen around ages 7-8, making second grade the appropriate time for formal money instruction.
learnerActions: Reveal each coin's value and a short fact (e.g. the dime is 'smaller than a nickel, but worth more').
Name each coin and state its cents value: penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢; then name the dollar bill (100¢) and state that 100¢ = $1.
Point out at least one pair where the smaller coin is worth more.
activities.intendedInsight: Each coin has a fixed cents value that must be learned, and a coin's size does not tell you its worth.

activities.title: Comparison and totalling checks with diagnostic distractors
feedback: When a learner picks the five pennies or says 'the same', treat it as the size/count heuristic and route back to laying coins over their proportional value; three dimes (30¢) is worth more than five pennies (5¢).
If notation is mixed (e.g. $0.50¢ or $5 for a nickel), show that $ and ¢ are not used together and that 5¢ means five cents.
A correct number with weak reasoning should be followed by 'show me why' using the coins.
activities.rationale: Comparison and totalling items with the count/size answer as the diagnostic distractor surface whether the size/number heuristic is still operating and check notation. A selected-response or slider item can reward a correct number without revealing the underlying reasoning, so pair these checks with the workbench or a 'show me why' follow-up rather than relying on them to fix the misconception.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 standard: solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately (e.g. if you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?).
learnerActions: Answer 'Which is worth more: three dimes or five pennies?' and explain the choice.
Total a mixed set such as '2 dimes and 3 pennies — how many cents?' and show the count.
Write the answer using ¢ (or $ with a decimal) without mixing the two symbols.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging worth by value — not by coin size or number of coins — and recording amounts in correct notation.

activities.title: Build the prerequisite number sense: skip-counting and place value
feedback: If the learner restarts counting at each new coin, reinforce counting on from the running total.
When switching from 25s to 10s to 1s breaks down, slow it on the number line and name the jump size each time.
activities.rationale: Chandler & Kamii attribute change-making difficulty to coordinating tens and ones (this source is marked unverified in the row), and the pedagogy recommends building skip-counting and place value before totalling mixed coins. This activity targets that prerequisite so the workbench and comparison tasks rest on secure counting.
sourceClaims: Giving change when payment is made with a dime is difficult for young children because of the difficulty of coordinating tens and ones — underlying the trouble children have switching counting patterns across denominations.
learnerActions: Skip-count aloud by 5s, 10s, and 25s on a number line or hundred-square.
Practise switching patterns mid-count: 25, 50, 75, then +10, then +1 (as if adding a dime then a penny).
Count on from a starting number rather than restarting at one.
activities.intendedInsight: Totalling mixed coins is a skip-count-and-switch task that depends on fluent skip-counting and place value.

constraints: When making a coin's worth visible, use a proportional representation (each coin shown as its worth in unit-squares) rather than relying on a realistic play coin, since a coin is not a concrete representation of its own value; real/realistic coins remain useful for diagnosis and handling.
Introduce denominations a couple at a time to limit how often the counting pattern must switch.
Build skip-counting (5s, 10s, 25s) and place value before totalling mixed collections.
Model 'counting on' from the largest coin and correct $/¢ notation, including 100¢ = $1.
A static denomination reference establishes facts but does not provide totalling or make-change practice; use it to support, not replace, hands-on value building.

Selected-response or slider checks can reward a correct number without revealing the size/count reasoning behind it; pair them with a 'show me why' step or hands-on value work. A check of this kind can assess totalling and comparison but does not itself elicit the proportional-value reasoning.
Real or realistic coins are useful for diagnosis and handling, but when teaching the size/worth contradiction, add a proportional value representation so worth is seen apart from size.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The Chandler & Kamii (2009) source is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about tens/ones coordination is carried forward with that caveat and should be re-checked before relying on it.

The legacy row rated role-play/dialogue and 3D as poor with absolute claims ('a 3D environment adds nothing', an 'in-role dialogue cannot show' the contradiction). These are catalog preferences, not established facts, and have not been reproduced as universal laws. A shopkeeper role-play can still provide authentic make-change practice if paired with a proportional-value representation; it is omitted here only as a lower-priority format, not as pedagogically impossible.

Arithmetic checked: 2 dimes + 3 pennies = 23¢ (counted 10, 20, 21, 22, 23); three dimes = 30¢ vs five pennies = 5¢; 30¢ built as three dimes or a quarter and a nickel; paying 46¢ for a 40¢ item gives 6¢ change — all consistent with the source and retained.
The source's make-change scenario pays 46¢ for a 40¢ item (change 6¢); this is logically consistent but oddly chosen, so the activity states item cost and payment explicitly to avoid ambiguity.

The row's parentTitle labels this 'Halves and quarters (age 7+)', which does not match the money objective; the original field is left unchanged and the guidance follows the money description and evidence statements.

probeDeeper: Three dimes or five pennies — which would you rather have, and why?
This dime is smaller than the nickel — how can it be worth more?
Show me 30¢ a different way, using different coins.
If I gave you one more dime, how much would you have now?
assess.correctAnswer: Totals 2 dimes + 3 pennies as 23¢ by counting 10, 20, then 21, 22, 23; states three dimes (30¢) is worth more than five pennies (5¢) and justifies by value, not size or number of coins; assembles 46¢ and gives 6¢ change; writes amounts using ¢ (or $ with a decimal) correctly without mixing the two.

errorPatterns.pattern: Value = size: a physically bigger coin is worth more — nickel beats dime, or five pennies beat three dimes because the coins are bigger or more numerous
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay each coin over its proportional value (dime = 10 unit-squares) so worth is seen apart from size; confront this preoperational value-equals-size heuristic directly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the bigger or more-numerous set as 'worth more'; on a total, treats the nickel as greater than the dime

errorPatterns.pattern: Value = count (unitary thinking): counts each coin as one, or counts all coins by ones regardless of denomination
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach that a coin's value is a number of cents you count on, using proportional manipulatives; start from one denomination before mixing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 2 dimes + 3 pennies is '5', or counts 1,2,3,4,5 touching each coin rather than counting on by value

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot switch counting patterns across denominations — skip-counts one coin but stalls moving from 25s to 10s to 1s when coins are mixed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise counting on from the largest coin, scaffolding the switch with a number line; reteach place-value-based counting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts 25, 50, 75 then adds a dime as '76' or restarts the count; overrelies on dimes to avoid switching

responseLevels.gap: Reasons by size or number — picks the bigger or more-numerous set as worth more and counts coins by ones; cannot total a mixed handful.
responseLevels.full: Counts mixed coins by value with 'counting on', judges worth by value not size or number (three dimes > five pennies, with justification), makes simple change, and writes amounts with $ or ¢ correctly — transferring to a new collection.
responseLevels.partial: Knows individual coin values and can total a single denomination, but stalls switching counting patterns for mixed coins or slips back to size/count on a comparison; totals only with prompting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out real or realistic coins. Ask three things and WATCH how the child counts: (1) 'Here are 2 dimes and 3 pennies — how many cents altogether?' (2) 'Which is worth more: three dimes or five pennies? Show me.' (3) 'This costs 46¢ — pay with these coins; now suppose it cost 40¢, give me the right change.' Watch whether they count by VALUE (skip-counting and switching patterns) or by size/number, and whether they write the amount with $ or ¢ correctly.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pitting three dimes against five pennies — fewer, smaller coins that are worth MORE — forces a choice between value-reasoning and the size/count heuristics: a child using size or number picks the pennies or says 'the same', while a value-reasoner picks the dimes and can show why. Watching the count on the 2-dimes-3-pennies task reveals whether they switch counting patterns or count every coin by ones.
